newsitem.title: FRANCE: Big increase seen in world online ad revenues.
newsitem.headline: Big increase seen in world online ad revenues.

text.p: The total revenues of on-line advertising on the Internet will grow rapidly and especially outside the United States, according to a study by Jupiter Communications.
The U.S.-based market research company said at the MILIA multimedia trade fair that online advertising revenue outside the U.S. was $6.1 million in 1996, or just 1.5 percent of the world total.

"However, slowly but surely, the Internet is starting to fulfil its promise as a worldwide phenomenon. Increasing PC penetration, telecoms deregulation, proliferation of native-language content, deployment of midband and broadband solutions -- these developments and others are driving growth in leading European and Asia/Pacific Rim countries," it said.
"Jupiter projects that (online) advertising revenues outside the U.S. will climb to $25 million in 1997 and $704 million in the year 2000," said Gene deRose, president of Jupiter.
"That's a move from 1.5 percent to 12 percent (of the world total) in four years", he added.

Jupiter forecasts that both the European and Asian/Pacific online ads markets, roughly equal in size in 1996, will take until the year 2000 to grow as big as the 1996 U.S. market, in which no major publisher was profitable.
By the year 2000, the European market will be 30 percent bigger than the online ad market in the Asia/Pacific Rim region.
In 1996, Japan, Britain, Germany and the Netherlands had the most developed online ad markets. Japan was the biggest with over $1.7 million in revenues.

By 2000, Jupiter said Germany and Japan will lead non-U.S. markets with over $200 million in ad spending each. Britain, Australia/New Zealand and all of Scandinavia will follow with over $50 million each.

That year, the American online advertising market will have grown to over $5 billion, Jupiter said. Online ad spending will however remain a small fraction of total ad spending with Jupiter putting the percentage at 2.6 percent in the U.S. in 2000.
